newsitem.title: ROMANIA: CLOSE CONTEST AS ROMANIANS VOTE FOR PRESIDENT.
newsitem.headline: CLOSE CONTEST AS ROMANIANS VOTE FOR PRESIDENT.

text.p: Romanians voted on Sunday in a close presidential election which could end President Ion Iliescu's seven years in power and symbolically finish the 1989 anti-communist revolt.
Iliescu, a senior official under dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, is running neck-and-neck with Emil Constantinescu, an academic who held no office under communism.
Polling stations should close at 9 p.m. (1900 GMT) but can continue to take in straggling voters until midnight (2200 GMT). Exit polls will be broadcast once all voting has ceased.
No commentator was willing to pick a winner after the first round two weeks ago gave the president a slender four-point lead over his challenger.

But voters signalled then that they wanted a change by throwing Iliescu's leftist party out of government for the first time since Ceausescu's 1989 overthrow and execution. A new centrist government is to be formed within days.

"If I am elected, I will not only be a new president but a different kind of president," Constaninescu said after being thronged by hundreds of supporters outside a polling station. "A president who will stay in touch with ordinary Romanians."

The opposition says leftists hijacked the 1989 revolution to seize power. They say victory will end Romania's status as the one Eastern European country where anti-communists have not held power and will finally improve the country's image abroad.

"I voted for Emil Constantinescu. I've been waiting for this all my life," Alexandra Negrici, 34, said in Timisoara, the town where the 1989 upheaval started. "If he wins, we will be able to say at last that the revolution has been completed."

Officials said turnout by mid-afternoon stood at 34 percent, virtually the same as in the opening round. Iliescu needs a high turnout to stay in office, particularly in the backward rural areas which traditionally support him.
Most voters queried in one village east of the capital said they had backed Iliescu.
Constantinescu, a geology professor, accuses Iliescu of seven years of corrupt mismanagement that has left Romanians in poverty with average monthly salaries of less than $100.

The president vowed during the campaign to shield Romanians against the excesses of market economics and told voters his rival would restore exiled King Michael and pre-war landlords bent on reclaiming their homes and closing factories.
"I believe I can be the best alternative in the present situation. A president needs experience," he said after chatting to voters outside a Bucharest polling station.
"I can ensure cooperation between the opposition and the government in the country's best interests. I am prepared for any alternative. I am a realistic politician and a fighter."

If he hangs on for another term, Iliescu will face a hostile cabinet committed to tax cuts and improved benefits combined with financial discipline to bridge the gap in living standards with near neighbours Hungary and Poland.
Constantinescu has won the backing of most political parties, including Iliescu's first post-1989 prime minister Petre Roman, who came third in the opening round.
He may also benefit from the negative campaigning style of the 66-year-old president who has reportedly been worn out by the election struggle.

Economist Radu Vasile, one of several prospects for prime minister, said he had received signals the opposition's victory in parliament was encouraging foreign investors to consider boosting the flow of much-needed funds to Romania.
